q: A primary alcohol is oxidised gently with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, and the product is distilled off as it forms. The product belongs to the class of:
x: RCH₂OH loses two hydrogens to give RCHO, an aldehyde; removing it at once stops further oxidation to the acid. Ketones come from secondary alcohols.

q: Ethyne is passed into dilute sulphuric acid containing mercury(II) sulphate at about 75 °C. The final organic product is:
x: Water adds across one π bond to give CH₂=CHOH (vinyl alcohol), which is unstable and rearranges to CH₃CHO. Ethanol would need two additions of hydrogen, not water; propanone forms from propyne, not ethyne.

q: Cyclohexene is treated with ozone and the ozonide is decomposed with zinc and water. The product is:
x: Cutting the ring C=C opens the ring, and each of the two carbons becomes a –CHO group on the same six-carbon chain. Splitting into two molecules forgets that the double bond is inside a ring; zinc prevents oxidation to acids.

q: 0.10 mol of but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃, undergoes ozonolysis (zinc and water work-up). What mass of ethanal forms? (CH₃CHO = 44 g mol⁻¹)
x: Each but-2-ene gives two CH₃CHO, so 0.20 mol × 44 = 8.8 g. Forgetting that both halves give ethanal gives 4.4 g; 5.8 g uses the molar mass of propanone.

q: Ozonolysis of an alkene, followed by zinc and water, gives butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, as the only organic product. The alkene is:
x: Joining two butanone carbonyl carbons with C=C gives CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, 3,4-dimethylhex-3-ene. Hex-3-ene gives propanal, 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene gives propanone, and 3-methylpent-2-ene gives butanone plus ethanal.

q: Methanal is made by passing methanol vapour and air over heated silver: 2CH₃OH + O₂ → 2HCHO + 2H₂O. What volume of oxygen at STP is used to oxidise 6.4 g of methanol? (CH₃OH = 32 g mol⁻¹, molar volume 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
x: 6.4/32 = 0.20 mol methanol needs half as much O₂: 0.10 mol × 22.4 = 2.24 dm³. Taking a 1:1 ratio gives 4.48 dm³.

q: But-1-ene is absorbed in cold concentrated H₂SO₄ and the product is warmed with water. The alcohol formed is then oxidised with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. The final organic product is:
x: Markovnikov addition puts –OH on carbon 2, giving butan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol, which oxidises to the ketone CH₃COCH₂CH₃. Butanal or butanoic acid would follow only if the –OH went to carbon 1 (anti-Markovnikov).

q: Aldehydes and many methyl ketones form white crystalline addition products when shaken with a saturated aqueous solution of:
x: The hydrogensulphite ion is a nucleophile that adds to the C=O carbon, giving a crystalline bisulphite compound. NaHCO₃ is the test for carboxylic acids, not carbonyl compounds.

q: Propanone is shaken with dilute aqueous NaOH (aldol condensation). The addition product is:
x: OH⁻ removes an α-H to give ⁻CH₂COCH₃, which adds to the C=O of another propanone: (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂COCH₃. 3-Hydroxybutanal is the aldol of ethanal; propanone has α-hydrogens, so it does not undergo a Cannizzaro-type reaction.

q: In the aldol condensation of ethanal with dilute NaOH, the species that attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second ethanal molecule is:
o: ⁻CH₂CHO, formed when OH⁻ removes an α-hydrogen
H⁻, transferred from another ethanal molecule
x: OH⁻ acts as a base and takes an H from the CH₃ next to the C=O; the carbanion (enolate) is the nucleophile. Hydride transfer is the key step of the Cannizzaro reaction, which needs an aldehyde without α-hydrogens.

q: In the Cannizzaro reaction 2HCHO + NaOH → CH₃OH + HCOONa, the oxidation number of carbon changes from:
x: HCHO: 2(+1) + C + (−2) = 0, so C = 0. CH₃OH: 4(+1) + C + (−2) = 0, C = −2. HCOO⁻: (+1) + C + 2(−2) = −1, C = +2. One molecule is reduced and one oxidised (disproportionation); swapping the two is the common slip.

q: Ethanal reacts with HCN (with a trace of base), and the product is then hydrolysed by heating with dilute acid. The final organic product is:
x: CN⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon to give the cyanohydrin CH₃CH(OH)CN; acid hydrolysis turns –CN into –COOH on the same carbon. Propanoic acid forgets the –OH; 3-hydroxy puts the groups on different carbons.

q: When a nucleophile adds to the carbonyl group of an aldehyde, the hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon changes:
x: The C=O carbon has three σ bonds and a π bond (sp², 120°). After addition the π bond is gone and the carbon has four σ bonds (sp³, about 109.5°). The reverse change happens in elimination.

q: 6.0 g of methanal is heated with concentrated NaOH and reacts completely by the Cannizzaro reaction: 2HCHO + NaOH → CH₃OH + HCOONa. What mass of methanol forms? (HCHO = 30, CH₃OH = 32 g mol⁻¹)
x: 6.0/30 = 0.20 mol HCHO gives 0.10 mol CH₃OH (2:1) = 3.2 g. Ignoring the 2:1 ratio gives 6.4 g; 1.6 g halves twice.

q: When an aldehyde is warmed with Fehling's solution, a red-brown precipitate forms. The precipitate is:
x: The aldehyde reduces the blue Cu²⁺ complex to Cu⁺, which separates as red Cu₂O. CuO is black, and Cu(OH)₂ is blue; silver metal, not copper, is deposited in the Tollens' test.

q: Propanone is warmed with iodine and aqueous NaOH: CH₃COCH₃ + 3I₂ + 4NaOH → CHI₃ + X + 3NaI + 3H₂O. The organic salt X is:
x: The CH₃ of the CH₃CO– group becomes CI₃ and is split off as CHI₃; the rest of the molecule, CH₃CO–, becomes the ethanoate ion. So the salt has one carbon fewer than the ketone. Sodium propanoate forgets that a carbon leaves as iodoform.

q: Ethanal is warmed with Tollens' reagent and a silver mirror forms. The organic product in the alkaline ammoniacal solution is:
x: Tollens' reagent is a mild oxidising agent: CH₃CHO is oxidised to CH₃COO⁻ while [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ is reduced to Ag. Ethanol would be a reduction product, the opposite of what happens.

q: Which reagent distinguishes ethanal, CH₃CHO, from propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO?
x: Ethanal has the CH₃CO– group and gives yellow iodoform; propanal does not. Both are aliphatic aldehydes, so both give a silver mirror, a red Fehling's precipitate and an orange 2,4-DNPH precipitate.

q: An aldehyde or ketone reacts with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine to give a coloured precipitate. This product belongs to the class of:
x: The –NH₂ of the reagent adds to C=O and water is lost, giving C=N–NH–C₆H₃(NO₂)₂, a hydrazone. Cyanohydrins come from HCN; the reaction is not an oxidation.

q: 0.88 g of ethanal is warmed with excess Fehling's solution: CH₃CHO + 2Cu²⁺ + 5OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + Cu₂O + 3H₂O. What mass of Cu₂O forms? (CH₃CHO = 44, Cu = 63.5, O = 16)
x: 0.88/44 = 0.020 mol ethanal gives 0.020 mol Cu₂O (1:1). M(Cu₂O) = 127 + 16 = 143, so 0.020 × 143 = 2.86 g. Using the 2 Cu²⁺ as 2 mol Cu₂O gives 5.72 g; 2.54 g is the mass of the copper only (0.040 × 63.5).

q: A compound C₅H₁₀O gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine, does not give a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent, and gives no yellow precipitate with iodine and NaOH. The compound is:
x: 2,4-DNPH shows a C=O group; no silver mirror rules out the aldehyde pentanal, so it is a ketone. No iodoform rules out CH₃CO– ketones: pentan-2-one and 3-methylbutan-2-one, (CH₃)₂CHCOCH₃, both have it. CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ has none.
